# Refurbishing an Old Distributor Cap

When a specific automotive part goes out of production, the standard procedure is to replace it. Distributor caps are generally low-cost items, often costing less than $20 new, so investing in them seems counterintuitive unless you are dealing with a classic vehicle where reproduction parts are scarce or nonexistent. However, if the core housing and rotor are intact, simply replacing the worn contact points can extend the life of the component without requiring a full swap. This process effectively refurbishes an old distributor cap by restoring its electrical integrity.

The primary failure mode in these components is usually wear on the breaker points or the carbon track within the distributor. In many older ignition systems, the points are mechanical contacts that open and close to interrupt the current flowing through the coil's primary winding. Over time, pitting, oxidation, or physical erosion reduces the gap tolerance, leading to inconsistent timing or weak spark generation. If you can access the internal mechanism without destroying the housing, a targeted repair is often viable.

Refurbishing this specific type of cap involves several mechanical steps that require precision tools rather than just basic hand tools. First, you must remove the rotor and the distributor cap itself from the engine bay. Once removed, inspect the shaft for play; if the shaft wobbles, the bearing or bushing inside the distributor is worn, and refurbishing the points alone will not solve the issue. Assuming the mechanical foundation is solid, the next step is to disassemble the point assembly.

The most critical component to address is the contact point set itself. These are typically held in place by a small screw or spring tension. You can purchase replacement point sets that match the specific geometry of your old unit. Once the new points are seated, you must carefully file them down to ensure they are perfectly flat and parallel. If one side is higher than the other, the gap will be inconsistent, causing the engine to misfire under load. Use a feeler gauge to set the exact specification provided in the factory manual for your vehicle model.

After setting the points, you must reassemble the carbon tracking system. This involves inserting the new carbon brush into its designated slot and ensuring it makes contact with the distributor shaft. The brush needs to be seated firmly but not so tight that it creates excessive friction on the rotating shaft. If the carbon track is damaged or missing segments, you can sometimes purchase a replacement sleeve or repair kit specifically designed for these older distributors.

The final step in the refurbishment process is reseating the cap. You must ensure that the internal terminals align perfectly with the rotor and the points before tightening the retaining clamp. A loose connection here can cause arcing inside the distributor, which will destroy the new points rapidly. Once reassembled, test the ignition system by checking for a strong, consistent spark at the plug wires. If the spark is weak or intermittent, the refurbishment may have been incomplete, or the coil itself may be failing due to the increased resistance in the circuit.

This approach transforms a disposable part into a functional component, saving money and preserving original hardware. It requires patience and attention to detail, particularly when filing the points and setting the gap. If you find that the internal shaft is seized or the housing is cracked, however, then replacement is the only logical path forward. For those interested in sourcing specific mechanical components or finding a dedicated community for classic car restoration, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide useful links to specialized forums or parts lists, though direct automotive suppliers remain the primary source for these physical items.
